title: Why Do Male Chimpanzees Throw Rocks at the Same Trees for More Than a Decade? - Nautilus
gist: Researchers describe 'accumulative stone throwing' — male chimpanzees repeatedly hurling rocks at the same trees over years, leaving gnarled bark scars and rock piles — as a rare, potentially cultural behavior documented in four wild chimpanzee groups at Boé National Park, Guinea-Bissau, and elsewhere in West Africa.

insights.claim: 'Accumulative stone throwing' — repeated rock-throwing by male chimpanzees at the same trees over more than a decade, producing gnarled bark scars and rock piles at the base — has been documented as a rare, potentially cultural (socially transmitted rather than purely instinctive) behavior in four groups of wild chimpanzees in West Africa.
insights.speaker: Ammie Kalan
insights.so_what: A candidate example of non-human cultural transmission (behavior passed socially rather than genetically), relevant to research on the evolutionary origins of culture and tool-adjacent behavior.
insights.quote: Accumulative stone throwing is a rare, potentially cultural, behavior that has been observed among four groups of wild chimpanzees in West Africa

insights.claim: The behavior has been observed at Boé National Park in Guinea-Bissau, where trees bearing gnarled scars and surrounding rock piles mark sites where chimpanzees have thrown stones over time, even after the animals have since left the area.
insights.speaker: Ammie Kalan
insights.so_what: Gives a specific field site where this rare cultural-candidate behavior can be studied or verified.
